Australia’s Answer To The Mustang: The Holden Monaro GTS

CA
By Chloe Adams Car Culture & Restomod Editor • via Silodrome Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Silodrome Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights

⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • CHLOE ADAMS Car Culture & Restomod Editor

Heritage Preservation vs Modern Performance

Automotive passion is increasingly defined by the synthesis of analog soul and contemporary engineering. This coverage from Silodrome illustrates how bespoke builders, private collectors, and restomod artists are preserving the golden eras of internal combustion while adopting carbon fiber composites and precision craftsmanship.

Big Picture: Auction hammer prices and enthusiast demand indicate sustained historical appreciation for rare, analog driver's vehicles.

This is a 1971 Holden Monaro GTS fitted with the desirable Australian-developed 5.0 liter (308 cubic inch) V8, a popular engine with enthusiasts, as it means the Australian car is powered by a locally-developed engine.

📌 The Core Development

The Monaro is one of the most iconic Australian cars ever made, it was an antipodean answer to wildly popular cars of the time, like the Mustang, Camaro, Javelin, Cougar, Firebird, Barracuda, and AMX. It become a racing legend in its own lifetime, and surviving examples are now hugely collectible.

Holden showed the Monaro to the press for the first time at Surfers Paradise Raceway in Queensland on July the 22nd, 1968. 11 weeks later, a privately entered Monaro GTS 327 won the Hardie-Ferodo 500 at Bathurst. Essentially Australia’s equivalent to the Indy 500. It was Holden’s first ever win in the race, and it wouldn’t be the last.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

The Monaro is one of the most iconic Australian cars ever made, it was an antipodean answer to wildly popular cars of the time, like the Mustang, Camaro, Javelin, Cougar, Firebird, Barracuda, and AMX. Image courtesy of General Motors Holden.

Ford’s XR Falcon GT, a four-door sedan with a 225 bhp version of the Mustang’s 289 cubic inch (4.7 liter) V8, had finished 1st and 2nd in the Hardie-Ferodo 500 race at Bathurst in 1967 – by far the biggest race in Australia.

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

At Ford’s archrival Holden, managing director Max Wilson and marketing director John Bagshaw pushed a two-door version of the new HK sedan range into production. Their case was easier to make because the coupe shared much of its body with the sedan, therefore development costs would be low and the development timeline would be short.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

Bagshaw also argued for Chevrolet’s 327 V8 so the car could take on the Falcon GT both on the track and on dealership showroom floors. Holden needed a real halo car, and the Monaro would soon become the Australian automaker’s most iconic (and desirable) model.

The shape of the new coupe came from Holden’s newly-built design center at Fishermans Bend in Melbourne. Ted Schroeder blended the roof into the rear fenders in a way that echoed the 1966 Oldsmobile Toronado, though it left rear passengers with almost no view out. Holden called the result the first sports machine designed and engineered in Australia.
